title: Log, semi-log, log-log and symlog views: does it follow a power or exponential law?
summary: The same data drawn on four axis types. A straight line on semi-log means an exponential law, a straight line on log-log means a power law, and symlog keeps zero and negative values visible.

media.alt: Four small plots of the same decaying points: linear-linear with points crushed at the corner, semi-log with a bent curve, log-log with a straight line and a fitted slope of -1.50, and a symlog panel of a signed curve with a shaded linear zone.
media.caption: Reference render of class F1.6 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: Does it follow a power or exponential law?
read_the_figure.axes: Top left: linear x and y. Top right: x linear, y logarithmic. Bottom left: both logarithmic, with a fitted dashed line and its slope in the legend. Bottom right: x linear, y symmetric-logarithmic with the shaded band showing the linear zone around zero, linthresh = 0.01.
look_at: Which panel makes the data a straight line, and what law does that mean?
In which panel can you not see the data at all, and why?
What is the slope printed on the log-log panel and what exponent does it give?
In the symlog panel, where does the curve stop being logarithmic and become linear?
as_drawn: The data are 25 points between x = 0.1 and 100 with y = 3 x^(-1.5) plus 6 percent noise.
The log-log panel prints 'fit: slope = -1.50' and draws the fit as a dashed line. The symlog panel states linthresh = 0.01 and shades the linear zone.
x and y span different numbers of decades (3 and 5), so the visual angle of the line is not 1.5. The printed slope, not the picture, carries the exponent.
read_the_figure.proves: That over the plotted range a power law describes the data with exponent about -1.5. It does not show the law holds outside the range, and over under about two decades many curves look straight.
if_wrong: A slope printed with no statement of how it was fitted (in log space, which points).
Symlog used without stating linthresh: the shape near zero cannot be reproduced.
A log axis that includes zero or negative values: they cannot appear and are silently dropped.

terms.meaning: One axis logarithmic. A straight line there means exponential growth or decay.
Both axes logarithmic. A straight line there means a power law.
A relation y = C x^m: doubling x multiplies y by the same factor 2^m for every x.
A factor of ten along a log axis. Equal lengths are equal ratios.
A scale that is logarithmic far from zero and linear inside a band around zero, so signed data fit on one axis.
The half-width of the linear band of a symlog axis.

remember: Straight on semi-log (y): exponential. Straight on log-log: power law, slope = exponent.
Log axes cannot show zero or negative values.
Equal distances are equal ratios, not equal differences.
Print the fitted slope, state how it was fitted, and state linthresh for symlog.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Points mark data. Position on a logarithmic axis encodes the logarithm of the value, so equal spacing means equal ratio. The dashed line is a fit in log-log space; its slope is the exponent. The shaded band on the symlog panel is the interval where the axis is linear.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: A power law y = C x^m becomes ln y = ln C + m ln x: a straight line of slope m. An exponential y = A e^(bx) becomes ln y = ln A + bx: straight on semi-log. Taking logarithms converts a curve whose type you must guess into a line, and a line is the one shape the eye judges precisely. The four-panel layout shows by contrast that only the log-log panel straightens these data.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Log scales squeeze large relative errors into small visual gaps. Any smooth curve looks straight over a short range. The slope printed from a fit depends on which points enter and on noise; the visible slope depends on how many decades each axis shows. A symlog axis distorts shapes near zero because it changes character at linthresh.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: A printed slope turns a visual impression into a number that can be compared. The linthresh statement is needed because symlog depends on it; without it nobody can redraw or check the plot. Both are in this render.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: To judge whether the slope is constant plot the local slope d ln y / d ln x against x, or plot y x^1.5 against x: a flat line means the law holds. For heavy-tailed data a log-log cumulative plot is better than a histogram. If the data change sign, symlog or an inverse hyperbolic sine scale; if you only need small changes near zero, stay linear.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a bottom strip that shows the residual of ln y from the fit against x, so a curve in the data shows up as a pattern. Draw a reference triangle with its slope written on it.

steps.title: Reading an exponent from two points
steps.tex: y=Cx^{m}\ \Rightarrow\ m=\frac{\log y_2-\log y_1}{\log x_2-\log x_1}
steps.note: At x = 0.1, y = 94.9; at x = 100, y = 0.003. Over 3 decades in x, y falls 4.5 decades: m = -4.5 / 3 = -1.5. C is the value at x = 1, about 3.

steps.title: The symlog transform (base 10)
steps.note: Matplotlib's default (linear scale 1, base 10). It is continuous at |y| = l, linear through zero, and logarithmic beyond: a signed quantity fits on one axis, at the price of a bend at plus or minus linthresh.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) which panel shows a straight line and what law is it? (2) Why is the linear panel useless? (3) What do the numbers on the log-log fit give?

solution.text: Bottom left (log-log) shows a straight line. The semi-log panel (top right) is bent, so the data are not exponential. Straight on log-log means a power law.
In the linear panel almost every point sits within a few units of zero; only the first 5 or 6 are visible away from the axis, because y spans five decades.
The legend prints slope -1.50: y is proportional to x to the power -1.5. Check from two points:

worked.answer: A power law y = C x^(-1.5) with C about 3: doubling x divides y by 2^1.5 = 2.83.

checks.q: What does a straight line on a log-log plot tell you that a straight line on a linear plot does not?
checks.hint: Take logarithms of y = C x^m.
checks.answer: A power law, with slope equal to the exponent. A straight line on linear axes means a linear relation.

checks.q: Two points on a log-log line: (2, 40) and (20, 0.4). What is the exponent?
A symlog plot of a smooth curve looks as if it has a sharp bend near zero. Real or artefact?
checks.hint: Where does the axis change character?
checks.answer: Artefact of the axis: the transform changes from linear to logarithmic at linthresh, which bends the shape. Check linthresh and plot on a linear axis near zero.
